title: Complex Planetary Nebula Sh2-71
caption: The planetary nebula Sh2-71, imaged by the Gemini North telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Gemini North view shows Sh2-71, a complex planetary nebula in the direction of Aquila. The brightest star near its center has long been assumed to be the star that created it, but some astronomers wonder whether a much dimmer, bluer star just to the right and slightly below might be the true parent.

Despite the name, a planetary nebula has nothing to do with planets. It is a shell of gas cast off by a star like the Sun late in its life, lit up by the hot, exposed core the star leaves behind. Knowing which star is the source matters, because that star's heat and light drive the glow of the gas around it.

The picture combines three narrow-band exposures, each lasting 15 minutes, taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Mauna Kea in Hawai‘i. Hydrogen-alpha light is shown in orange, ionized helium (He II) in blue and oxygen ([O III]) in cyan, so the colors map where different gases glow.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North. Hydrogen-alpha is shown as orange, He II as blue and [O III] as cyan.
understand.eye: Each narrow filter isolates the glow of one kind of gas, and the long exposures gather far more light than the eye.

explore: This is one of Gemini's Legacy images. It covers 5.3 by 3.6 arcminutes of sky and is rotated 110 degrees clockwise from the usual north-up orientation, so the layout on screen differs from how the nebula sits on a standard sky chart.
alt: A complex planetary nebula with a bright star near its center and a dimmer, bluer star just below and to the right.
